parts.content_target: Compare insulation materials using water-cooling data and a fair investigation. Read scales accurately and record appropriate precision.
parts.credit_requirement: Plot cooling data: axes/units (1), accurate points (1), suitable trend line (1).
parts.prompt:
Plot these water-cooling measurements on the blank grid and draw an appropriate curve. Time/min: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Temperature/°C: 80, 72, 65, 59, 54, 50.

![Blank cooling grid](visuals/VIS-6117-12-02-learner.svg)
parts.canonical_answer: Axes: time/min horizontally from 0 to 10, temperature/°C vertically over a suitable range such as 20–90. Plot (0,80), (2,72), (4,65), (6,59), (8,54), (10,50) accurately and draw a smooth decreasing curve through or close to the trend without unjustified oscillations. The answer panel is separate from the blank learner grid.
marking_guidance: Suitable evenly scaled axes with both quantities and units (1).
All six points within ±1 °C vertically and appropriate horizontal plotting tolerance, normally half a small square (1).
Suitable smooth decreasing trend, not an arbitrary zigzag or oscillation (1).

parts.content_target: Compare insulation materials using water-cooling data and a fair investigation. Interpret and evaluate observations and experimental data.
parts.credit_requirement: Calculate cooling rate over a supplied interval: temperature change/time (1), value and unit (1).
parts.prompt: Calculate the average cooling-rate magnitude for the uninsulated water from 2 to 6 min using the data 72 °C at 2 min and 59 °C at 6 min.
parts.canonical_answer: Temperature decrease = 72 − 59 = 13 °C; interval = 6 − 2 = 4 min. Average cooling-rate magnitude = 13/4 = 3.25 °C/min. The signed temperature gradient is −3.25 °C/min.
marking_guidance: Temperature change divided by elapsed time, 13/4 (1).

3.25 °C/min as magnitude, or −3.25 °C/min clearly identified as signed gradient (1). Exact supplied-data answer is 3.25; accept 3.0–3.5 only when a permitted graph read-off is explicitly used, with follow-through.

parts.content_target: Compare insulation materials using water-cooling data and a fair investigation. Describe and explain experimental arrangements and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: State a thermometer measures the temperature (1).
parts.prompt: State the instrument needed to measure the water temperature in this investigation.
parts.canonical_answer: A thermometer or suitably calibrated temperature probe.

parts.content_target: Compare insulation materials using water-cooling data and a fair investigation. Plan an investigation with predictions, suitable apparatus and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: Plan insulation comparison: same vessel/water volume (1), same starting temperature (1), vary only insulation material (1), record temperature at fixed times (1), repeat/control ambient conditions (1), compare cooling curves for a conclusion (1).
parts.prompt: Plan an investigation to compare two insulation materials by measuring how water cools. Decide what to keep constant, what to measure, how to repeat the experiment and how to reach a conclusion. Include safe handling of hot water.
parts.canonical_answer: Use identical vessels and 100 cm³ water portions, each starting at 80 °C. Fit equal-thickness jackets of the two materials with the same covered area and identical lids. Place them in the same 22 °C surroundings away from differing draughts. Position thermometer bulbs in the water without touching glass and record temperatures at fixed times, for example every two minutes for ten minutes. Repeat each arrangement and compare mean cooling curves or temperature drops; the smaller drop indicates better insulation under the test conditions. The teacher supplies the hot water, vessels stand on heatproof mats and handling avoids burns. Predict that a more effective jacket gives a smaller temperature fall.
marking_guidance: Vary material while controlling thickness/covered area/lids (1).
Record temperature at fixed times with suitable apparatus (1).
Compare cooling curves or drops for a conditional conclusion (1). Safety and a sensible prediction are expected supporting plan details; no invented extra marks.
